claim_1.claim: ELISA analysis of serum from 56 healthy volunteers after primary vaccination (day 0) and secondary vaccination (day 21) showed anti-spike IgG responses in all but three individuals after primary vaccination (day 0), significant boosting after secondary vaccination (day 21), no gender-associated difference, and an inverse correlation between neutralizing antibody response and age.

sources.quote: Primary vaccination induced binding antibody and neutralizing antibody responses in all but three individuals; these responses were boosted significantly after the secondary vaccination (Fig. 1a, b, Extended Data Fig. 1b–d).
Here we used systems tools to analyse immune responses in 56 volunteers (Extended Data Table 1) who received two doses of BNT162b2 (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

claim_2.claim: Neutralizing Antibody Titer Assay analysis of serum from 56 healthy volunteers showed robust neutralizing responses against wild-type WA1/2020 after primary vaccination (day 0) that were significantly boosted after secondary vaccination (day 21), declined about twofold by days 90–120, were inversely correlated with age, and in day-42 serum from 30 participants showed about 10-fold lower neutralization of B.1.351 than WA1/2020.

sources.quote: Primary vaccination induced binding antibody and neutralizing antibody responses in all but three individuals; these responses were boosted significantly after the secondary vaccination (Fig. 1a, b, Extended Data Fig. 1b–d).
The neutralizing antibody response reduced about 2-fold by days 90–120, this being comparable to the response to the Moderna mRNA-1273 vaccine9 (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1c).

BNT162b2 vaccination also induced a neutralizing antibody response against the B.1.351 variant of concern, albeit at a tenfold-lower magnitude than against the wild-type WA1/2020 (WA1) strain (Fig. 1c, Extended Data Fig. 1f), consistent with previous studies11.
Here we used systems tools to analyse immune responses in 56 volunteers (Extended Data Table 1) who received two doses of BNT162b2 (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

claim_3.claim: Flow Cytometry analysis of PBMCs from 38 vaccinated individuals showed spike-specific polyfunctional CD4 and CD8 T cell responses were more readily detectable seven days after the secondary immunization (day 28) than earlier time points, with CD4 responses primarily T-helper-1 type, dominant IFNγ and TNF responses in CD8 T cells, and no significant correlation with age or neutralizing antibodies.

sources.quote: Vaccination also stimulated spike-specific T cell responses, which were more readily detectable seven days after the secondary immunization (Fig. 1d, e, Extended Data Fig. 2a–e).
Consistent with previous studies3, the CD4 T cell responses were primarily of the T-helper-1 type, although there was a low-level T-helper-2 (IL-4) response (Extended Data Fig. 2b).

IFNγ and TNF were the dominant responses in CD8 T cells; three individuals with no known exposure to SARS-CoV-2 responded even at baseline, suggestive of CD8 T cells that are cross-reactive to related viruses, as has previously been shown12 (Extended Data Fig. 2d).
There was no significant correlation between T cell responses and age or neutralizing antibodies (Extended Data Fig. 2f–k).
Here we used systems tools to analyse immune responses in 56 volunteers (Extended Data Table 1) who received two doses of BNT162b2 (Extended Data Fig. 1a).

claim_4.claim: CyTOF analysis of whole blood from 27 vaccinated individuals showed that intermediate monocyte (CD14+ CD16+) frequencies increased significantly two days after the primary vaccination (day 2) and were substantially higher two days after the secondary vaccination (day 23), while pSTAT3 and pSTAT1 levels increased in multiple cell types one day after secondary vaccination (day 22) relative to one day after primary vaccination (day 1).

sources.quote: We first assessed whole-blood samples of 27 individuals using cytometry by time of flight (CyTOF).

The frequency of intermediate monocytes (CD14+CD16+ monocytes) increased significantly two days after the primary vaccination, and was substantially higher two days after the secondary vaccination (Fig. 2b, Extended Data Figs. 5d, 6).
In addition, there were enhanced levels of phosphorylated (p)STAT3 and pSTAT1 in multiple cell types on day 1 after secondary vaccination, relative to day 1 after primary vaccination (Fig. 2c, d).
Days 1 and 7 were compared against day 0; days 22 and 28 were compared against day 21.

claim_5.claim: Olink analysis of plasma from 31 vaccinated individuals showed significant increases in IFNγ and CXCL10 on days 1 and 2 after primary vaccination (days 1 and 2) versus baseline, with further increases after secondary immunization (day 21); plasma IFNγ was 11.3-fold higher at day 22 than day 1, CXCL10 peaked at day 23, IL-10 showed a similar but non-significant trend, and IFNγ levels correlated with pSTAT1 and pSTAT3 across several cell types.

sources.quote: To further investigate this phenomenon, we measured plasma cytokines in 31 vaccinated individuals using Olink (https://www.olink.com/products/target/inflammation/).
Of the 67 cytokines detected, the concentration of 2 cytokines (IFNγ and CXCL10) were increased significantly on days 1 and 2 after primary vaccination (Fig. 2e left).
Similar to our observations on intermediate monocytes and pSTAT1 and pSTAT3, the concentrations of these cytokines were increased even further after the secondary immunization (Fig. 2e right).
The concentration of plasma IFNγ was 11.3-fold higher at day 22 relative to day 1 (Fig. 2f).
CXCL10 peaked on day 23 (Extended Data Fig. 7a).
The anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 showed a similar trend with enhanced response following secondary immunization, although this did not reach statistical significance (Extended Data Fig. 7b).
Furthermore, there was a correlation between plasma IFNγ levels and pSTAT1 and pSTAT3 expression levels across several cell types (Fig. 2g, h, Extended Data Fig. 7e).
Days 1 and 7 were compared against day 0; days 22 and 28 were compared against day 21.

claim_6.claim: Bulk RNA-seq assay analysis of whole blood from 31 participants, with 6 of 185 samples removed after quality control, showed that secondary vaccination (day 21) induced a greater transcriptional response than primary vaccination (day 0), including nearly a fourfold increase in differentially expressed genes at day 22 versus day 1, enrichment of antiviral and interferon modules after both doses, broader induction after the boost of dendritic cell activation, Toll-like receptor signalling, monocyte and neutrophil modules on days 22 and 23, age-associated differences on day 22, and significant associations between day-22 IFNγ and interferon/inflammatory modules.

sources.quote: Next, we performed bulk mRNA sequencing of whole blood from 31 participants. Six of 185 samples did not pass quality control and were removed from the analysis (Extended Data Fig. 8a, b).

Secondary vaccination generated a greater transcriptional response (as has previously been seen in a recent study of adjuvanted hepatitis B vaccine17), with nearly a fourfold increase of differentially expressed genes at day 22 as compared to day 1 (Fig. 3a); this is consistent with the increased markers of innate immunity detected by both CyTOF and Olink (Fig. 2).
Gene-set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed that both doses of BNT162b2 stimulated antiviral and interferon response modules18 (Fig. 3b).

In addition to the induction of antiviral pathways, secondary vaccination led to increases in signatures of dendritic cell activation and the upregulation of Toll-like receptor signalling, monocyte and neutrophil modules on days 22 and 23 (Fig. 3b, Extended Data Fig. 8c, d).

On day 22, younger participants tended to have greater changes in monocyte and inflammatory modules, whereas older individuals had increased expression of B and T cell modules (Extended Data Fig. 8g).
Both interferon and inflammatory modules were significantly enriched by GSEA when using genes ranked by correlation with IFNγ on day 22 (Fig. 3c).
Days 1, 2 and 7 were compared against day 0; days 22, 23 and 28 were compared against day 21 in a, b.

claim_7.claim: CITE-seq analysis of 45 PBMC samples from 6 individuals showed emergence one day after secondary vaccination (day 22) of cluster C8, a CD14, VCAN, CD1C, FCGR1A and CD274 myeloid population expressing WARS, GBP1, IFI30 and IFITM3, which increased from about 0.01% of Lin− HLA-DR+ cells on day 1 after primary vaccination (day 1) to about 1% on day 22, contributed to interferon and monocyte blood transcriptional modules, contained classical monocyte, cDC2 and intermediate monocyte subclusters, showed higher IRF1, STAT1, STAT2, STAT3 and IRF8 with lower FOS, JUNB, JUND and ATF3, correlated with plasma IFNγ, and was accompanied by broader interferon induction across cell types and natural killer cell activation on day 22.

sources.quote: We performed cellular indexing of transcriptomes and epitopes by sequencing (CITE-seq) of 45 peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) samples from 6 individuals (Extended Data Fig. 1a) to disentangle these two effects and to examine transcriptional changes at the single-cell level.
Notably, cluster C8 (which expressed CD14, VCAN, CD1C, FCGR1A and CD274 mRNA or protein) emerged on day 22, one day after secondary vaccination (Fig. 4b).

These cells uniquely expressed interferon-stimulated genes, including WARS (also known as WARS1), GBP1, IFI30 and IFITM3 (Extended Data Fig. 9d), and constituted about 0.01% of the Lin−HLA-DR+ population on day 1 after primary vaccination but increased almost 100-fold to about 1% one day after secondary vaccination (Fig. 4c).

Iterative removal of each cluster from a pseudobulk score showed that C8 contributed to the increased interferon as well as monocyte blood transcriptional modules (BTMs) that we observed in the bulk transcriptomics data on day 22 (Extended Data Fig. 9e).

C8 was a heterogeneous mix of classical monocytes (C8_0, C8_1 and C8_3), a classical dendritic cell subtype (cDC2; C8_2) and intermediate monocytes (C8_4), as evidenced by proximity to the original clusters calculated by Euclidean distance (Fig. 4e, Extended Data Fig. 10d–f).

C8 had a relatively higher expression of IRF1, STAT1, STAT2, STAT3 and IRF8 and reduced levels of FOS, JUNB, JUND and ATF3—the same transcription factors that defined the monocyte population in the previous study25 (Fig. 4g).
Notably, the emergence of C8 correlated with plasma IFNγ levels (Extended Data Fig. 10g, h).

In addition to the emergence of C8, our CITE-seq analysis demonstrated that the interferon signature was broadly induced across cell types on day 1 and day 22, and the higher magnitude of response on day 22 was more evident (Fig. 4i).

Furthermore, there was activation of natural killer cells on day 22, as observed by downregulation of natural-killer-cell-associated gene modules, and upregulation of AP-1 transcription factors26 on day 22 (Extended Data Fig. 10k, l).
Days 1 and 7 were compared against day 0; days 22 and 28 were compared against day 21.
